content.thinking:
I need to build this module carefully in one pass without testing along the way, so I'm planning the design first: an elven ranger roughly 1.85m tall, standing in a relaxed A-pose with the bow held in the model's left hand based on the reference image orientation.

Now I'm working out the skeleton structure using absolute world coordinates to avoid confusion with local joint space—placing hips around y=0.98 and building a spine chain upward through several catmull-interpolated points to the neck base, making sure the root joint comes first and the chain has the right number of named segments to match the control points.

Continuing up, I'm chaining the neck joints onto the chest, then placing head and jaw joints with appropriate forward-down aim directions, estimating head proportions (roughly 7.5 heads tall) to keep the stylized anime look consistent for the elf character.

Now I'm working out the arm chains in an A-pose: shoulder, elbow, and wrist joint positions on both sides (mirrored by sign), with the elbow angled down-outward and the wrist curving slightly forward, forming a two-span chain from shoulder to wrist tip.

I'm continuing to leg joints, defining hip, knee, ankle, and toe positions for a four-point three-span chain, mirrored left and right, and parenting the arm chain to the chest joint in the spine.

Now I'm setting boots and feet to sit flush with the floor at y=0, with ankle height around 0.09, and planning a torso sweep along the spine chain using a loft with an elliptical radius profile for the body shape.

Working out belt geometry...

I'm sketching the torso radii at various heights—hips, waist, chest, shoulder—to taper the silhouette realistically, then planning a slightly curved vertical path using a few control points rather than a straight line.

For the tube's orientation, I'm using the x-axis as width and z-axis as depth, treating the path as roughly vertical with linear interpolation from t to y. For the paint, I'm defining a green tunic with gold trim, including a thin gold centerline where the x-coordinate is very close to zero.

I'm adding a leaf embroidery decal to the chest using an SVG texture applied onto the torso sweep surface, and then planning hanging tunic panels at the hips as extruded shapes with pointed hems front and back.

Still figuring out panel placement...

I'm planning the garment structure with overlapping pointed front panels, a back panel, and a draped cape without a hood, mimicking an asymmetrical tunic silhouette.

For the cape itself, I'm building a back plate as an extruded polygon that widens from the shoulders to a jagged hem, tilted so the bottom swings backward, plus considering a swept shoulder mantle connecting across the neckline.

Still shaping capelet outline...

Collar extends to 1.66 with cape hanging off the back plate. Now I'm sketching the head: a skull sphere at the head center with skin coloring, plus a small jaw sphere positioned lower for the chin, building the anime-style face from skull and jaw primitives.

For height, I'm checking that the chin-to-crown span works out to roughly 1.88 total body height with feet at zero. Then I'm placing eye decals on the skull surface using angular offsets from the head center, with mirrored positioning for left/right symmetry and green iris coloring.

For the nose I'm using a tiny cone decal, and for the mouth I'm working out surface geometry on the skull/jaw ellipsoid to find the right z-depth at a given y-offset below center, trying a surface ray approach since the jaw sphere overlaps the naive calculation there.

Now I'm designing elf-style ears as extruded leaf-shaped outlines pointing outward and slightly up, checking the ordering of outline points to make sure the shape doesn't self-intersect.

Now I'm building the hair as swept locks using catmull paths with taper and gradient coloring, plus a partial sphere hair cap positioned over the skull's crown and back to avoid covering the face.

Working through the geometry, the hairline at 28° elevation lands correctly on the forehead above eye level. I'll rotate the cap -35° about x to tilt its pole backward, and size the cap slightly larger than the skull, positioned a bit toward the back of the head.

For the bangs, I'm planning tapered side locks that start at the hairline and sweep down past the temples to around chest height, positioned just outside the eye azimuth so they frame the face and pass in front of the ears.

For the rest, I'm thinking through back hair strands—around a dozen sweeps flowing from the crown down toward the waist with some sway, parented to the head joint since long hair can just move rigidly with it rather than needing its own bone chain. I'm computing starting and midpoint positions for each strand procedurally, interpolating x-offsets across the width of the head.

Now I'm checking whether the hair geometry clips through the cape/capelet at the back—since both occupy similar z-depth near the shoulders, I need to push the hair further back (more negative z) or shrink the capelet's depth so the hair visibly layers on top rather than intersecting it.

I'm defining the cape's z-position as a function of height, offsetting the hair slightly behind it so they don't intersect, and checking that the cape hem and capelet scale stay clear of the hair strands too.

For the hair strands, I'm widening them into flat ribbon shapes using elongated ellipses so they merge into sheet-like locks, spacing roughly 12 strands across a spread of about ±0.17 with a wavy offset, including some locks draped in front of the shoulders.

Now I'm checking where those front locks need to clear the capelet and torso geometry, solving for the ellipse radii at different heights so the hair sits just outside those surfaces rather than clipping through them.

Checking the sleeve layering now - cream inner sleeve, brown leather bracer on the forearm, fingerless gloves on hands - and figuring out how to blend the colors along the arm using arc-length-based bands.

Adding bracer rods with gold ring caps at elbow and wrist, then designing the hands as fingerless gloves: palm box, finger capsules, and thumb with skin-toned tips. I'm positioning the wrist and hand joints for the hanging A-pose, with the left hand gripping the bow through a rod passing through the curled fist.

Now I'm working out the bow's orientation in 3D space -- limbs curving in the vertical plane with tips angled back toward the archer so the string faces inward, while the grip bows slightly outward away from the body.

I'm adjusting grip and tip positions so the bow aligns with the hand, matching wrist z to hand center and nudging lower tip near the floor without forcing contact, then working out wrist and elbow coordinates for the gripping arm.

Now I'm computing the arm segment lengths and fist position, then laying out the bow's curved path through tip, limb midpoints, and grip using catmull interpolation, along with limb thickness tapering and a thin string rod connecting the tips.

Writing bow coloring...

Now I'm positioning the quiver on the back, tilted behind the right shoulder, working out cylinder dimensions and endpoints that clear the hair and cape geometry.

I'm working out a draped chest strap by computing points along the torso's surface profile, running a diagonal from the right shoulder over the top to the left hip, then a second strap from the back toward the quiver.

Since the capelet hangs outward and covers the torso above y≈1.4, I'm having the strap emerge from beneath it, running from roughly (-0.11, 1.38) down to (0.14, 1.02), sampling points along the ellipse surface to keep it hugging the body. I'm also planning a crossing strap and a pair of tapered waist belts as torus rings.

Now I'm adding details like a brown belt with a gold diamond buckle, a dagger scabbard angled on the left hip positioned to clear the thigh and tunic panel, a pouch on the back right hip, and considering a leather corset overlay with a bust band sweeping across the belts.

I'm shaping the corset as a second vertical sweep from y 1.1 to 1.36 with slightly larger radius, leather-painted with stitching and lacing, and rigging it to a spine joint around y 1.2 for simplicity since it should stay rigid at rest.

For the legs, I'm planning brown tapered pants with gold diamond knee guards, tall brown boots with flared knee cuffs and pointed toes, and a leg sweep whose radius narrows from hip to knee to ankle.

Still working out foot geometry...

With four points (hip, knee, ankle, toe), the joint chain maps naturally: hip, knee, and ankle joints each aim toward the next point, with the toe as the terminal tip joint. I'm setting the ankle to the leg's third joint and the toe to the chain's tip, then sweeping the leg skin along this path with varying radii from hip to knee.

I'm figuring out the leg sweep's radius crop so the taper ends appropriately near the ankle, checking that the hip's circular cross-section fits reasonably within the torso's hip boundary even if slightly extending past the sides. Now I'm planning gold-buckled thigh straps as small brown torus shapes wrapped around the thigh, oriented along its vertical direction.

Calculating the exact position for the thigh strap by interpolating the leg's chain parameter and radius profile, then placing the torus with a small tube radius and factoring in a slight tilt from the leg's lean. Next I'm sketching a knee guard as a diamond-shaped extrusion positioned at the front of the knee.

Moving on to upper body elements, I'm adding a gold chest clasp, planning green short sleeves over cream undersleeves with gold trim rings at the shoulder, and setting up the neck area using the skin shader.

For the neck itself I'm defining a two-segment chain path rising from the chest with increasing radius toward the head, placing an explicit head joint at the top of the neck, then starting the skull geometry with a scaled sphere positioned around head center coordinates.

Now I'm working out the jaw and chin with a small sphere scaled to taper the face, placing eyes at a calculated azimuth on the skull surface with slightly oversized anime proportions, and confirming eyebrows and lashes are included by default before moving on to the front hair bangs.

I need to adjust the hairline tilt so the fringe doesn't overlap the eyebrows -- checking angles to find a tilt and thetaLength that keeps the front edge safely above the brow line.

Now I'm positioning bang locks that sweep across the forehead and temple, calculating start points on the cap's curved surface so they emerge naturally from the parting rather than floating off the scalp.

I'm figuring out hair strands behind the ears connecting crown to the back mass, then settling on a pale silver-blonde palette with a lit and shadow tone, using a cel-shaded gradient paint per strand so tips darken slightly toward the mid color.

For the circlet, I'm skipping a hat and instead adding a thin gold leaf band sweeping around the forehead at brow height, computing the arc's radius using the cap's elevation angle so it hugs the head curvature properly.

I'll risk the ring overlap and keep the circlet as is, maybe simplifying to a modest braided accent if needed. For the ears, I'm positioning pointed elf ears at the sides, checking how the hair cap's lower edge interacts with the ear's vertical span to see if it partially covers them.

Working through the math, the ears actually poke up into the hair just slightly, but that's fine—elf ears are supposed to peek out through the hair, so I'll leave them sticking through naturally. I'm also sketching in a small mouth line using a surface ray calculation, though I'm wary it might be too risky to get right.

Working out eye decal placement and mirroring using the hit position and surface, then moving to blush and hand geometry — palm boxes with glove coloring positioned along the forearm direction for each side.

Still defining the fingers...

Rather than fuss over exact finger wrap geometry around the grip, I'll simplify: give both hands the same relaxed, slightly curled finger pose, and position the bow grip rod right through the left hand's palm center so it reads as gripped without needing precise per-finger paths.

Still working out finger curl coordinates...

Still computing finger joint positions...

Still building finger and hand geometry, then moving to the quiver and arrows -- a cylindrical body with a gold rim ring, plus seven rod shafts protruding at an angle with small feather fletching cards attached.

Computing arrow positions...

Defining feather vane geometry...

For the shafts, I'm planning dark wood rods with flat caps sticking out of and into the quiver, plus thinking through strap details for the quiver itself.

Now I'm working out the cape's back plate shape with a jagged hem, using orthogonal direction vectors to orient and scale the outline so the cape hangs down from shoulder height to about 1.1 units below.

Continuing to plot the jagged hem points down to the cape's bottom edge, alternating sharp notches on either side to create a ragged torn-cloth silhouette, while checking it doesn't cross itself or collide with the hanging arms.

Now I'm checking that the cape's width and hem placement clear the limbs geometrically, then moving to the paint layer -- defining a green cel-shaded base with a gold embroidered trim along the hem, using a gradient that darkens toward the bottom and a vertical dashed vine pattern near the edge.

The cape's back face naturally faces away from the key light, so it stays in shadow tone consistently—that's the cel rule working correctly. For the gold embroidery detail, rather than computing a procedural cell pattern, I'm switching to a simpler approach: overlay an SVG vine decal texture on a plane positioned against the cape's back surface.

I'm computing the plane's outward normal by cross-multiplying the cape's local axes, then offsetting it slightly outward along that direction so the decal sits just above the cape surface without clipping into it.

I'm sizing the vine decal to fit the cape's taper, picking a 0.4 by 0.7 plane centered around y=-0.5 so it stays within the cape's width at both the narrower top and wider bottom, and making sure the textured decal only renders on the front-facing side.

Now I'm working out the tunic's front panels—extruded plates with gold-bordered leaf trim—defining the outline coordinates for overlapping pointed panels so I can calculate the border paths accurately.

I'm checking that the panel geometry flares outward enough at the hem to avoid clipping the thighs and knees, tilting the direction vector slightly to create a tunic-like drape. For coloring, I'm considering adding slim gold trim along the panel edges rather than a full border fill, since the distance-based edge test would get complicated otherwise.

Writing trim helper function...

For decoration, I'll skip leaf decals and just rely on trims, maybe adding a small vine texture plane on each panel positioned near the lower portion.

I'm computing the correct outward-facing normal for each panel plane using cross products of its local axes, then offsetting the plane slightly along that normal so it sits just outside the panel surface. I'm also adding a back tunic panel and a cape plate shape positioned behind the legs, defining its vertices and orientation vector, without worrying about gold trim interaction for now.

Now I'm planning to reuse that panel function with trim added, skip a left hip slit panel for simplicity, and color the torso tunic green over a cream underlayer. I'm adding a gold collar ring at the neck and a gold trim torus around the capelet rim, working out the torus radius, tube thickness, and scaling so it matches the capelet's lathed profile and sits at the correct height and depth.

Realizing lathe geometry doesn't support a scale parameter directly, so I need another way to flatten the circular cape shape -- maybe reducing the rim radius so it doesn't float too far in front of the chest, or building it instead from a swept elliptical loop, or mutating the mesh's scale.z after creation relative to its attachment point.

Since the mesh sits in world-aligned local space when the joint quaternion is identity, scaling along z should correspond to world z, so I can squash the lathe shape by adjusting its local scale without worrying about rotated bone axes complicating things.

Actually since Part exposes a scale option, I can set it directly as `capelet.scale.set(1,1,0.72)` after building it as a lathe geometry, positioning it at the right bone offset.

Still working out torus scaling...

Actually, scaling the torus anisotropically distorts the tube badly, so I'll switch to sweeping closed Catmull-Rom ellipse curves instead for belts, rims, circlet, and straps—building a reusable ring helper that generates elliptical point sets and sweeps a thin tube along them.

I'm defining the torso path with slight z-offsets near zero, mapping a y-position to radius through a piecewise linear profile function, then building the torso sweep as a Catmull-Rom curve through hip-to-shoulder points bound to the hip/spine bones, with a rounded cap at the top.

For coloring I'm splitting the torso paint by height: pants brown below the belt around y=1.07, tunic green above it, implemented as a conditional cel-shaded paint function. I'm also setting up the leg palette with distinct browns for pants, boots, and darker leather trim.

Defining the full color palette...

Adding gold rings to the bracer...

I'm setting up the arm chain with shoulder, elbow, and wrist joints as a polyline path, using smooth blending between the segments to fill out the limb geometry.

Still writing hand function...

Computing the palm end position at roughly (0.40, 0.856, 0.105), then working out the curled finger joint positions and grip center relative to the palm, checking thickness offsets so the fingers wrap naturally around the grip.

Now I'm setting up the straight-finger pose for the right hand, with slight curl offsets at each joint, and then positioning the thumb on the body side using mirrored x-offsets for left versus right hands.

Each finger becomes a bone chain attached as a child of the arm's wrist joint, with named segments for each phalanx and a "digit" role tag.

I'm defining the sweep thickness bands for skin versus glove coverage along each limb, then tallying up total joint counts across legs, arms, fingers, spine, and head to confirm the rig stays around 55 joints total. Now I'm setting the neck's sweep radii before tapering toward the head.

Next I'm placing the jaw joint and sphere part with specific pivot and aim points for the hinge, deciding against adding teeth, and confirming the head joint orientation. I'm checking that torso lofting can reference the hips and spine chain together as a mixed bone list, then noting the collar sits under the capelet before moving on to boot definitions.

For each leg, I'm laying out the hip, knee, ankle, and toe points per side using a mirrored x-offset, choosing a polyline sweep over catmull for crisper bend angles. I'm setting a five-key radius taper from thigh to ankle and confirming the boot sweep radius stays slightly larger than the leg radius so it properly overlays the shin without clipping.

Now I'm checking the thigh positions on both legs — at x=.1 with radius .092 the inner edges nearly meet at center with a small .016 gap, which looks fine. Then I'm computing the boot upper cuff geometry: finding the interpolated point along the knee-to-ankle line at y=.47, setting flat-capped rod endpoints from that point down to the ankle, and tapering the radius from .07 at top to .056 at bottom so it sits just outside the leg radius at that height.

I'm adding a flared collar cuff from y=.47 down to .40 with radius .082, wider than both the leg and boot shaft so it visually hides the boot top seam. For the foot, I'm sweeping a tapering path from ankle to a pointed toe tip, with radius shrinking from .052 to .03 and the end cap extending into a dome to form a pointed boot toe.

I'm placing a dark leather heel block beneath the boot, adding a gold diamond-shaped emblem on the front of the cuff, and sketching a closed ring sweep around the ankle for a strap detail.

Now I'm adding thigh straps using a loop-ring helper at two heights across the leg, with small gold buckle boxes positioned at the front of each strap, matching the paired-strap look from the reference.

Checking the tube radius against the ring position confirms the strap embeds nicely into the leg surface without gaps. I'm sketching a helper function that interpolates the leg's centerline position at a given height, returning the x,z coordinates needed to place each ring along the limb.

Now I'm calculating the thigh and knee geometry: checking the small axis tilt, computing the pants radius at the knee joint, and positioning a gold knee-guard plate flush against the front of the leg. I'm working out a diamond-shaped outline for that plate's silhouette using sharp corner points.

I'm noting the plate will float slightly at its edges since the knee surface curves away laterally, but that's acceptable for a decorative guard. I'm also considering adding tiny glowing emerald gem accents to the circlet, pommel, buckle, and other hardware using the glow helper.

Now I'm working out how to add small glowing green rune studs along the bow, likely by sampling points along the bow's sweep path and placing small glowing spheres at each one.

I'll rig the bow to the wrist joint using the sweep's bone weighting, then paint gold banding along the bow's length with a custom paint function creating gold rings at specific t-values plus a central grip section.

The grip region gets a leather overlay with slightly larger radius. I'm defining the bow's base color as dark green with gold striping logic, using positional conditions based on surface normal to place a gold edge line along the front-facing belly of the curved bow.

Writing bow sweep radius array...

Now I'm adding the bowstring as a thin tube connecting the tip points, computing brace height from the gap between grip and string, then checking that the bow's position doesn't collide with the arm or hand.

Next I'm checking that the bow tips clear the cape geometry — comparing the cape's hem height and depth against the bow's lower tip position, confirming no overlap. Then I'm starting to position the dagger scabbard at the hip, laying out the rod endpoints for its shape.

Now I'm adding a hip pouch on the opposite side from the sheath, positioning a small box with a gold clasp against the thigh so it hangs naturally outside the torso radius.

For the chest strap, I'm sampling points along the torso's elliptical cross-section from shoulder to hip, checking the radius stays within bounds, and giving the strap a rounded cross-section rather than a flat ribbon shape.

I'm adding a second thinner strap crossing from the opposite shoulder to hip for a harness look, plus gold buckle accents at the midpoints. For the corset, I'm working out a thickened sweep profile between y 1.14 and 1.37 with a slight radius offset to sit over the straps convincingly.

Now I'm interpolating a profile table across the waist region to get a smooth hourglass taper, with belt rings positioned at specific heights using radius and depth values derived from that table.

For the pants, I'm checking that the hip bulge width stays reasonable relative to the torso radius so legs don't look disproportionate under the tunic panels. I'm also setting up the corset as a swept ring following a vertical path with radius offsets from the body profile, with flat end caps and front lacing painted along the centerline.

For the lacing pattern, I'm adding cream cross-stitch diagonals over the base leather color near the front seam, then checking the shoulder and capelet geometry -- lathing the capelet outline from a joint near the chest, coloring it green, and adding a gold rim ring at the capelet's base to match its radius and verify it properly overlaps the torso below.

Now I'm tracing where the arm emerges from under the capelet hem, confirming the shoulder position sits within the capelet radius so the arm appears to come out from beneath it, then checking whether the front hair locks poke through or sit correctly against the capelet's curved surface at various heights, comparing their x/z positions against the capelet's radius profile as it narrows toward the top.

I'm now defining the back hair strands as a set of paths, parameterizing each strand's starting x-offset and plotting control points that curve down the back of the head, over the cap, and around the capelet shoulder area.

I'm checking for overlap between the hair strand tip and the quiver at y1.02 — both end up occupying the same z-range near -.345 to -.40, so I need to reposition the quiver base to y 1.1 and z -.45 to avoid the collision.

I'll adjust the quiver's back position slightly to avoid the hair collision, pulling it outward a touch, and skip adding extra straps for now to keep things simple. For the hair strand, I'm defining a curved ribbon path with tapering radius along its length and setting up the orientation so it follows the vertical sweep naturally.

Working out spacing between strands and verifying overlap at top versus bottom, then adding a subtle sine-based wave offset and varying end lengths per strand based on their horizontal position.

Checking that the control points for the hair curve don't collapse into duplicates at the edges, and adjusting the z-depth formula so hair sitting above the capelet still follows the head's curvature correctly.

I'm adjusting the cape plate's attachment point so it meets the capelet without gap or intersection, redefining capeZ to shift the top closer. I'm also deciding to skip the circlet ring since the cap geometry is uncertain, opting instead for a simple gold forehead band or gem placement.

For the forehead gem, I'm casting a ray from front of the head to find a surface hit point on the skull/cap union, then attaching a small gold cone-shaped gem with a glow there, falling back to skipping if the ray misses. I'm also considering draping a closed ring of points around the head at that height onto the surface to form a thin circlet, pulling each sample toward the nearest skull/cap surface point.

Now I'm placing that gold circlet at a slightly higher height so it sits above the ears without clipping the hair, then starting on forehead bangs — a handful of hair strands sweeping from the crown down across the forehead toward the temples, while being careful they don't droop low enough to cover the eyes.

I'm checking the strand coordinates against the skull's ellipsoid surface and realizing one of the points falls outside the head bounds, so I need to pull that strand point back in to keep it hugging the scalp correctly.

Checking the tuft endpoint against the skull surface confirms it sits right at the surface at that point, slightly brushing the brow outer edge—likely acceptable since bangs sweeping over the forehead sides matches the reference. I verify the second point lands correctly too, and move to check the starting point near the crown.

Now I'm working out the hairline cap placement—its center and scale relative to the skull dimensions—and considering the eye decal positioning around it. The expression reads calm, consistent with the reference. Then I shift to defining the cap sphere's radius and scale needed to fully cover the skull top.

Since it's nearly spherical, rotation won't distort the shape much, so I don't need to worry about which part faces where. I'm setting up the cap as a partial sphere geometry with the scale applied before rotation so the pole stays correct, and deciding to skip extra details like hair parting strands or decals since the smooth shaded cap will read fine. Now I'm thinking about defining a vine pattern texture for the cape panels.

Writing SVG code...

I'm placing cape plane decals centered along the back plate, working out the position using an up-direction vector tilted slightly toward the back so the panel orientation follows the character's curve correctly.

Checking the plane width against the hem's actual taper at different heights, I realize my side plane positions don't quite match the cape outline—need to adjust so they sit inside the hem rather than poking out, so I'll apply a rotation to better align them.

Now I'm settling on a leaf size and position that keeps the overflow minimal, since a tiny sliver outside the hem is acceptable as long as the texture has an alpha cutout for the leaf shape. I'm also planning similar vine planes for the side panels, and adding small embroidered leaf decals on the chest of the tunic, mirrored on either side.

Repositioning the chest decals onto the corset surface instead, since the corset (covering torso y 1.14–1.37) would otherwise hide them. I'm computing where the corset surface sits at x=±.06 so the decal faces outward correctly, and noting the tunic is only visible in a thin band above the corset before the capelet covers it — then moving on to a small gold gem detail on the belt buckle.

Positioning the diamond-shaped gem plate on the belt front, adjusting its z-depth to sit flush against the belt/tube profile. Adding green iris coloring for the eyes and a small box-geometry decal for the mouth stick, then starting to work out the strap radius.

Now I'm mapping out bone references—hips, spine chain joints, chest, neck, head, jaw, and the left/right leg arrays—so I can loop over symmetric limb pairs using a side flag. I need to be careful only to import and use helpers like inkLines, cel, and animeEye that actually get referenced, since unused imports or variables will throw type errors.

Defining body profile curves...

Confirming the catmull points are evenly spaced so the arc-length parameterization stays linear, and checking how the hip root at .98 relates to the torso bone list — the first segment maps to the hips' weighted region. The hip-to-leg transition at y=.95 and the rounded cap at y=.88 for the pants crotch both look fine structurally.

I'm writing a loopRing helper that generates a closed ring of points for a given radius and center, then sweeps a catmull curve through them with a specified bone and six-sided cross-section. I need to figure out typing for the bone parameter — rather than importing a Joint type, I'll just alias it locally as the return type of the hips joint so everything stays in scope. Writing capelet outline...

Adding cape plate extrusion details...

For the backside, I'm checking whether the dot product with the light direction puts it in shadow, so I want the fold stripes to still read visually distinct even on the dark side rather than going uniformly flat. I'm defining separate flat backside colors for base, fold-dark, and highlight tones, then wiring the cape paint logic to pick gold for the wall edge or these shaded greens depending on front/back face.

Now I'm building a reusable panel helper for the tunic that extrudes an outline along given axes with a color and bone binding, plus optional gold trim rods along each edge for finishing detail.

Defining outline point types and skipping bevel to avoid issues with sharp concave corners, keeping thickness small and using simple circular rod sections for trim.

Now I'm checking panel placement — positioning the front panel at the hip/belt area so it clears the thigh bulge radius, verifying z-offset keeps it outside the torso and pants geometry, and confirming the trim thickness along the normal sits properly in front.

Then I'm setting up decal planes for the leaf texture: positioning two front panels at offset coordinates with different sizes and one back panel, computing the normal direction from the cross product of the local X and Y axes for correct orientation.

For the back panel I'm flipping the trim offset sign so decorative trim sits on the outer side, matching where the torso back is positioned. After the tunic hems and belt pouch, I move to the quiver geometry—a tapered tube with leather coloring and gold bands painted as rings along the axis.

For the arrow bundle, I'm computing a perpendicular basis from the quiver axis so I can place each arrow shaft radially around a central point in a circular arrangement.

Each arrow is a thin rod from a bottom point to a top point along the axis, with a wooden shaft color, and I'm adding fletching vanes near the top by building a small outline positioned slightly below the tip using the perpendicular vectors.

I'm also planning simpler details like a hidden quiver pouch at the hip, and considering a small decorative braid near the model's temple with beads along it.

Checking the braid position against the capelet's tapered silhouette to make sure it stays outside that boundary at each height, then catching that it overlaps the right front lock near x -.14, z .13 — so I need to shift that lock further out toward x -.2 to clear the collision.

I'll drop the right-side lock entirely and keep the braid asymmetric, with just a shorter lock behind it on that side, while the big lock stays on the left — the asymmetry actually reads better. I'm adding ten beads along the braid sweep and a small gold sphere to cap the tied end, skipping ear joints since they're unnecessary, and defining a reusable glow-gem helper (an octahedron with a teal glow) to scatter accent gems across the forehead, belt buckle, quiver rim, knee guards, dagger pommel, bow grip, and capelet clasp.

I'm placing a gold diamond clasp with a gem at the capelet's front hem, working out its exact position against the capelet's curved rim geometry. Then I'm adding forearm bracers on both sides, layering cream sleeve cuffs over the tapered arm tube so the wrist end stays slightly smaller than the bracer that covers it, with the palm style kept as fingerless leather gloves showing skin at the tips.

I'm sizing the bracer rod radii to match the forearm taper at roughly 38% past the elbow, adding thin gold rings at both ends, and skipping extra vine trim and pauldron details for now. For the upper arm I'm adding a green sleeve rod from shoulder to mid-arm that overlaps the cream lower sleeve underneath, capped with a small gold trim ring, keeping the skin-toned arm chain smooth beneath it all.

Now I'm working out the leg chain, with a toe tip joint and foot sweep anchored to the ankle joint, parented under the hips. I'm defining the spine as a small catmull-rom chain of three named points curving slightly forward and up, parented to the hips, then attaching the neck to the top spine joint, the head to the neck, and the jaw to the head — placing a small flattened sphere for the jaw geometry near the chin.

I'm figuring out where the nose and mouth should sit by ray-casting onto the skull or jaw surfaces, computing where the skull curve intersects the facial z-depth at the nose height, then placing a tiny skin-toned sphere for the nose and sizing the eye decals so they're spaced symmetrically without overlapping at the center.

Now I'm shrinking the eyes slightly, checking shadow coloring derived from skin tone, confirming fingertips and feet use the right materials, and verifying the sweep function signature for applying pants color along the leg geometry.

Thinking through how to place small rune gems along the bow using positional tube sampling -- trying to figure out which orientation counts as the bow's "front" face so the ornaments land consistently on the outward side rather than guessing at an arbitrary clock angle.

Writing bow paint logic...

Adjusting the grip position along the bow path so the z-coordinate aligns with where the fists hold it, tweaking the curve points accordingly.
